Project Mode.Purpose: Tracks pipeline runs for one compartment over time, so you do not pick every input file by hand between stages. A project holds one baseline, zero or more scans, and zero or more diffs.
Project Mode.Baseline: The first scan of a compartment. A project has exactly one baseline. Stage 1, 2, 3, and 4 (SLAM, Level, Cleanup, Segment) run once for the baseline. Stage 4 is optional.
Project Mode.Scans: Later scans of the same compartment, done to check for new damage. Each scan runs its own Stage 1, 2, 3, and 4. Add a scan with the 'New Scan' button. A scan needs its own raw source file, separate from the baseline's.
Project Mode.Diffs: A comparison between two cleanup outputs. Each diff runs Stage 5, 6, 7, and 8 (Diff, Classify, Surface, Export). A diff can compare a scan against the baseline, or against an earlier scan - so the same scan can show total change since the baseline, and separately, change since the last check. A diff's own M3C2 comparison (Stage 5) prefers Stage 4's (Segment) classified output for a side once that side has completed Segment, and falls back to Stage 3's cleanup output otherwise - When Segment also wrote the copy without the points outside the room (<name>_envelope_filtered.ply), the diff uses that copy, so the junk outside the room does not go into M3C2. Add a diff with the 'New Diff' button.
Project Mode.Pipeline selectors: Two dropdowns near the top of the main window pick which pipeline the stage buttons act on. 'Source pipeline' picks the baseline or a scan, for Stage 1, 2, 3, and 4. 'Diff pipeline' picks a diff, for Stage 5, 6, 7, and 8. The status label next to them shows each picked pipeline's next stage.
Project Mode.Manual mode: Every stage dialog also works with no project open, or with 'Use manual file selection instead' checked inside the dialog. Browse to input files by hand, same as before project mode existed. No project.json file is written in manual mode.

Units.Centimetres: Small length values show in centimetres (cm). Examples are voxel sizes, distance thresholds, cluster gap tolerances, M3C2 scales, the registration RMS, the Stage 7 recipe values and the damage detail radius. Each of these fields has (cm) in its label.
Units.Metres: Range values show in metres (m). These are the min range override and the map max range in Stage 1. Each of these fields has (m) in its label.
Units.Files: The scripts, the KISS-ICP configuration file, project.json, the M3C2 parameter file, CloudCompare and the USD files all use metres. The application changes centimetres to metres before it starts a script. Do not change the values in these files to centimetres.
Units.Check: Before a run, the application examines each centimetre value. If a value is very small or very large, the application asks you to confirm it. A frequent cause is a metre value in a centimetre field. For example, 0.05 in a centimetre field is 0.5 mm, not 5 cm.

Stage 1: SLAM.Purpose: Builds a 3D point cloud map and computes sensor trajectory poses from a raw lidar capture. Two backend options: Ouster CLI (reads raw sensor packets directly) or KISS-ICP (a different algorithm entry point, reads already-decoded PointCloud2 rosbag topics directly - works even when Ouster CLI can't read the same bag, since it doesn't need raw packets).
Stage 1: SLAM.Inputs:
- Backend: Ouster CLI or KISS-ICP
- Source: a .pcap capture, an .osf file, a ROS1 .bag file, or a ROS2 bag folder (containing .db3 + metadata.yaml) - both backends auto-detect the type. In project mode, this is filled in automatically from the picked pipeline's raw imported source (the baseline's, or a scan's). Picking a ROS2 bag folder here also checks it for raw Ouster packets - see What to expect.
- Meta JSON file (required for Ouster CLI + .pcap, optional/backend-dependent otherwise)
- [Ouster CLI] Voxel size in meters, visualizer toggle
- [KISS-ICP] Config .yaml (strongly recommended - see What to expect), optional voxel size override, optional min range override (see What to expect - useful when the sensor sees part of its own mount), optional dataloader/topic overrides
Stage 1: SLAM.Outputs: A single .ply point cloud map, saved to the path you choose. In project mode, this run's result is recorded on whichever pipeline is picked under 'Source pipeline' (the baseline, or the picked scan) - not on any other scan.
Stage 1: SLAM.What to expect:
Processing time scales with capture length. The map's orientation is arbitrary either way - neither backend has a gravity/leveling step, so the map inherits whatever tilt the sensor had at the very first frame. That's expected, not a bug - Stage 2 (Level) corrects it.

KISS-ICP specifically: without a config file, its defaults assume vehicle-scale outdoor odometry (max_range=100m) - confirmed on real data to under-populate an indoor map by roughly 190x (2,628 points vs. 503,189 points on the same capture, with vs. without a properly scaled config). The KISS-ICP config field defaults to the bundled 'kiss_icp_config_indoor.yaml' (already tuned for this project's compartment scale) if it's sitting next to the applet - double check it hasn't been accidentally swapped for a ROS bag's own metadata.yaml, a different file that happens to share the same common filename. Both per-point deskewing and sensor calibration have been separately verified correct when reading PointCloud2 rosbag topics - the point-count issue is purely the default config scale, not a data-quality problem.

KISS-ICP min range override: a robot-mounted sensor can see part of its own mount hardware. This can happen on a stable platform just as much as an unstable one - platform stability affects drift, not this. Each of these near-sensor points sits at the same spot next to the sensor in every single frame. Added together, they can form a dense, solid-looking blob of noise near the sensor in the final map. They can also confuse the SLAM solver: the solver may read this fixed, unmoving blob as real unmoving geometry, and align each frame to it instead of to the room. This can show up as a map that looks noisy, or as a map with the wrong shape. The min range override removes points closer than the set distance, before SLAM runs. Start with a small value, for example 0.2 to 0.3 meters, and raise it only as far as needed - a value set too high also removes real nearby room detail, not just mount noise. The 'This config's own min_range' label shows the current config file's own value, so you can tell whether a run used a value from the config or your own override.

Picking a ROS2 bag folder as Source checks its metadata.yaml for a decoded PointCloud2 topic. Some captures record raw Ouster sensor packets instead, to save bandwidth on the Jetson during capture and transfer - KISS-ICP needs a PointCloud2 topic and cannot read raw packets directly. If the check finds raw packets and no PointCloud2 topic, the dialog asks you to confirm a conversion, regardless of which Backend is selected - Ouster CLI can already read raw packets directly, but a decoded copy is still offered since it stays useful for comparing backends side by side or for use outside this pipeline. On yes, it runs decode_raw_packets.py; once the run finishes with no error, the decoded bag becomes this pipeline's SLAM input automatically (recorded on the pipeline itself, still tracked in project.json) in project mode, or fills Source directly in manual mode. A 'Check Source for Raw Packets...' button next to the field runs the same check by hand, for a path typed in instead of browsed to. This conversion step has been confirmed working end to end against real hardware data: a real capture decoded 748 scans from 47,906 lidar packets with 0 packets skipped.

Map max range: use this field to remove far noise, for example in open areas. The saved map does not include points that are farther than this distance from the sensor. SLAM registration still uses the full range. The field applies to both backends. For KISS-ICP, do not decrease max_range in the config file for this purpose. In KISS-ICP, max_range also removes map points that are far from the robot. The saved map then keeps only the area near the last robot position.

Map max horizontal distance and map max vertical distance (KISS-ICP only): these limits are like the map max range, but they are in two directions. The horizontal distance is along the floor. The vertical distance is up or down from the sensor. Use a horizontal limit to remove far noise in an open area and keep a high ceiling. 'Vertical' is the up direction of the sensor at the start of the scan. A point must be in all of the limits that you set.
Stage 1: SLAM.Next steps: Take it into Stage 2 (Level) to correct any tilt before cleanup. Both backends can point at the same source with different output filenames, for side-by-side comparison of map quality.

Stage 2: Level.Purpose: Corrects the SLAM map's arbitrary tilt so the floor is horizontal and sits at Z=0. It finds the floor plane with RANSAC, then rotates the cloud to match.
Stage 2: Level.Inputs:
- Raw SLAM output .ply (auto-filled from Stage 1's own recorded output, in project mode)
- Output .ply path
- Distance threshold, max planes to search, min plane size - the RANSAC tuning knobs
- Horizontal threshold - how close to vertical a plane must be to count as floor/ceiling at all (see What to expect)
Stage 2: Level.Outputs: A leveled .ply, rotated so the detected floor plane is horizontal and translated so it sits at Z=0.
Stage 2: Level.What to expect: The tool output lists every candidate plane found, its height (Z position), and whether it cleared the horizontal threshold. The floor is picked as the LOWEST candidate that clears this threshold, not the biggest one - a real ceiling can have more points than a real floor (a cleaner surface, with less clutter on it), so picking by size alone can pick the ceiling by mistake. If the chosen floor has very few points, or the console shows a low-horizontality warning or a fallback warning (no candidate cleared the threshold at all), check the result visually in CloudCompare before trusting it.
Stage 2: Level.Next steps: Open the leveled cloud in CloudCompare to confirm the floor genuinely looks horizontal now. Then use it as the input to Stage 3 (Cleanup).

Stage 3: Cleanup.Purpose: Removes noisy outlier points from a raw SLAM map using Statistical Outlier Removal (SOR), and optionally fine-aligns it onto a baseline map with ICP to correct residual drift.
Stage 3: Cleanup.Inputs:
- Input .ply to clean (auto-filled from Stage 2's own recorded output, in project mode)
- SOR neighbor count and standard deviation threshold
- Optional: baseline .ply to align onto. In project mode, if the picked pipeline is a scan, a 'Use Project Baseline' button fills this from the project's own baseline cleanup output - the usual choice, since a later 'vs. baseline' diff needs this scan aligned to the real baseline. Manual mode still has its own separate registered-baseline dropdown.
- Output .ply path (you choose this - CloudCompare saves exactly there)
- Optional: also register this output as a manual-mode baseline for a compartment name (a separate mechanism from a project's own baseline - see What to expect)
Stage 3: Cleanup.Outputs: A cleaned .ply file at the exact path you chose. If alignment ran, CloudCompare also resaves a throwaway copy of the baseline in the same folder (a CloudCompare CLI limitation, not an extra result to worry about) and auto-generates a registration log .txt (RMS, transformation matrix, point counts). In project mode, the RMS value and the RMS sidecar's path are also recorded directly on this pipeline's cleanup stage entry.
Stage 3: Cleanup.What to expect:
CloudCompare names the output file itself when it runs (its own auto-naming, not a filename you chose) - the applet detects whatever new .ply appeared after the run and renames it to the path you asked for. An earlier version tried to force an exact filename directly via a CloudCompare flag, but that proved unreliable in real testing (inconsistent in both directions across separate runs) - this detect-and-rename approach replaced it and has held up in testing since.

'Register this output as a manual-mode baseline' and a project's own baseline are two different things. A project's baseline is the project's own record, tracked in that project's project.json - nothing extra to register. The manual-mode registry (baseline_registry.json) is a separate, standalone lookup that only matters when no project is open.
Stage 3: Cleanup.Next steps: Open the cleaned .ply in CloudCompare to confirm the alignment looks right, and check the RMS in the registration log - lower is better. If this output IS a compartment's baseline (nothing to align it to), that project's baseline pipeline already IS the record that matters - no extra step needed.

Stage 4: Segment (optional).Purpose: Optional stage. You can go from Stage 3 (Cleanup) directly to Stage 5 (Diff); Stage 5 then uses the Stage 3 output. Without Stage 4, the points outside the room are not removed before M3C2, and Stage 8 cannot show surface names on the damage sites. Classifies a cleaned cloud's own points into floor, ceiling, individual walls, and unclassified, using segment_planes.py - the same RANSAC plane-finding approach Stage 2 (Level) uses, extended to keep every detected surface rather than just the floor. Runs once per baseline/scan pipeline, right after Cleanup - not per diff, since it describes ONE cloud's own structure, not a comparison between two clouds. Stage 5 (Diff)'s own M3C2 comparison prefers this stage's classified output once it has completed for a side, and falls back to Stage 3's cleanup output otherwise for that side.
Stage 4: Segment (optional).Inputs:
- Cleaned .ply, ideally leveled first (auto-filled from Stage 3's own recorded output, in project mode)
- Distance threshold, max planes, min plane size, horizontal threshold, max horizontal Z span - the same RANSAC tuning knobs Stage 2 (Level) exposes, plus two extra ones this stage needs since it keeps every surface, not just the floor
- Stray-point cluster filter (on by default) and its gap tolerance / minimum point count
- Split-plane merge (on by default) and its normal-similarity / distance tolerances
- 'Also write each surface as its own separate .ply file' checkbox, off by default (see Outputs)
- 'Flag unclassified points that sit outside the room as junk' checkbox, on by default, its margin field, and an 'Also write a separate copy with outside-envelope points removed' checkbox, on by default (see What to expect)
- Output folder (not a single file - see Outputs)
Stage 4: Segment (optional).Outputs: Written into one folder. By default, only a combined <name>_classified.ply (every input point, carrying a 'classification' field naming which surface it belongs to, an 'is_envelope' field, and an 'outside_envelope' field - see What to expect), a <name>_envelope.ply (the classified surfaces only, no interior/clutter - a ready-made input for Stage 7/Surface's unified shell reconstruction), and a manifest.json summarizing both. '<name>' is the output folder's own name, so files from different runs stay distinguishable even when opened outside their own folder. Turn on 'Also write each surface as its own separate .ply file' to also get one cloud per detected surface (<name>_floor.ply, <name>_ceiling.ply, <name>_wall_1.ply, and so on) and a <name>_unclassified.ply (points that matched no surface) written alongside those - useful for visually tuning parameters per surface, or so each surface becomes its own separate object in Omniverse. 'Also write a separate copy with outside-envelope points removed' is on by default. It also writes <name>_envelope_filtered.ply: the combined cloud without the junk points (see What to expect). Stage 5 (Diff) uses this copy. If no point is outside the room, the copy is not written, because it is the same as <name>_classified.ply. In project mode, this stage's recorded 'output' is <name>_classified.ply specifically; the envelope path, the surface list, the classification ID mapping, and the outside-envelope filter's own results are recorded directly on this pipeline's segment stage entry, the same way Stage 3's RMS gets copied in - manifest.json does not need to be read separately once a run is recorded.
Stage 4: Segment (optional).What to expect:
The floor/ceiling/wall classification is a straightforward height-and-orientation heuristic, not a tuned one - if a wall gets misclassified as ceiling or vice versa, check it against the surface list in the run report. If a real wall seems to be missing, turn on the separate-surfaces checkbox and re-run, then check the <name>_unclassified.ply cloud for a flat-ish cluster of points rather than a scattered one - that is usually the missing wall, broken up by clutter or debris stuck to it, not lost data. You can also check <name>_classified.ply's own 'classification' field (0 = unclassified) without turning that checkbox on at all.

Outside-envelope junk filter: every point classified as floor, ceiling, or a wall already describes the room's own shape. Any point NOT classified as one of those - the 'unclassified' points - can be real interior clutter or damage, or it can be scan noise from beyond the walls. This filter checks each unclassified point against the room's own footprint (worked out from the detected floor/ceiling/wall points) and height range, with some margin for slack near real walls. A point that falls outside both counts as likely junk and gets a new 'outside_envelope' field set to 1 in <name>_classified.ply. A point that falls inside keeps 'outside_envelope' at 0 - this covers both real interior clutter and every detected surface's own points. No point is ever removed from <name>_classified.ply because of this field - it is a label, added so you can filter or color by it later, not a deletion. Raise the margin field if real clutter near a wall is getting flagged by mistake; lower it if real junk near a wall is getting missed. If the run report says the filter was skipped, not enough floor/ceiling/wall surface was detected that run to work out a room footprint at all - check the surface list first.
Stage 4: Segment (optional).Next steps: Open <name>_classified.ply in CloudCompare and color by the 'classification' field to confirm the surfaces look right. Color by 'outside_envelope' to check the junk filter's flags before trusting them - if real content is getting flagged, raise the margin and re-run. Use <name>_envelope.ply as the input to Stage 7 (Surface) for a single unified shell reconstruction across floor/ceiling/walls together, instead of reconstructing each one as a separate disconnected mesh patch.

Stage 5: Diff (M3C2).Purpose: Runs M3C2 (multiscale model-to-model cloud comparison) to compute point-level distances between two clouds, highlighting where a compartment has changed between a reference and a comparison scan.
Stage 5: Diff (M3C2).Inputs:
- Baseline .ply and Comparison .ply. In project mode, these auto-fill from the picked diff's 'reference' and 'comparison' - the reference can be the project's baseline, or an earlier scan; the comparison is always a scan. Manual mode still has its own browse fields and registered-baseline dropdown.
  For a Stage 4 (Segment) output, use the file with the note 'outside-room points removed' (<name>_envelope_filtered.ply). It does not have the scan noise and the returns from beyond the walls, which can show as false damage. If you select <name>_classified.ply and the copy exists, Run asks which file to use. Click Yes to use the copy.
- Registration RMS from Stage 3 (auto-fills from the comparison side's recorded icp_rms in project mode; type it in, or click 'Load from Stage 3', in manual mode)
- Normal scale / Search scale / Search depth
- M3C2 parameters .txt file - either generate one directly with 'Generate Params File...' (uses the four values above plus a confirmed-working reference for everything else), or browse to one made via CloudCompare's Plugins > M3C2 Distance dialog
Stage 5: Diff (M3C2).Outputs: Multiple .ply files - CloudCompare saves every loaded cloud, not just the M3C2 result. The result (the one with an M3C2 distance scalar field) is usually the sparser, more colorful-looking cloud; the others are unchanged copies of the input clouds. This is a known CloudCompare CLI quirk, not a setting we can turn off. In project mode, the applet detects the real result file and records it, along with the params file used and the registration error used, on the picked diff's own diff stage entry. The diff also records the two input files that it used (reference_input and comparison_input). Stage 8 uses reference_input to put surface names on the damage sites.
Stage 5: Diff (M3C2).What to expect: A run report pops up after each successful run identifying which output is which. If generating the params file, remember Search scale and Search depth need to be set proportionally to Normal scale by hand - CloudCompare's own 'Guess params' doesn't update them automatically if you change Normal scale afterward, which caused a rounded/blunted-edges result in testing before this was caught. The run report shows for each input if the points outside the room were removed.
Stage 5: Diff (M3C2).Next steps: Open the result cloud in CloudCompare, set its active scalar field to 'M3C2 distance', and check the color scale (red = positive change, blue = negative, magnitude = degree of change). Then use it as the input to Stage 6 (Classify).

Stage 6: Classify.Purpose: This stage removes scan noise from the M3C2 result. It keeps only the points that show real change. By default, it also groups the real-change points into separate damage sites, so a false-positive point with no neighbors does not count as damage.
Stage 6: Classify.Inputs:
- M3C2 diff result .ply (from Stage 5 - must have the distance scalar field; auto-filled from Stage 5's own recorded output, in project mode)
- Distance threshold in meters (or use 'Load RMS & Suggest Threshold' to compute one from Stage 3's saved registration RMS)
- Cluster settings (on by default): method (DBSCAN or HDBSCAN), cluster gap tolerance, cluster density, and minimum damage-site size. Turn clustering off to use the threshold alone, as before.
- Keep all points (on by default): keeps every point and adds flag fields, so Stage 7 can make a full surface. Turn it off to keep only the flagged points.
Stage 6: Classify.Outputs: By default ('Keep all points' on), a .ply with every point and flag fields - see below. With 'Keep all points' off, a .ply containing only the points that passed both the threshold and the clustering check (the distance field is preserved, so Stage 7's coloring still works unchanged). A 'cluster_id' field marks which damage site each point belongs to. With 'keep all' checked, every point is kept, with a 'classified' field (1 = passed the threshold, 0 = did not) and a 'cluster_id' field (-1 = not part of a confirmed site). When clustering is on, a matching '.clusters.json' file is also saved, listing each damage site's centroid, point count, size, and average/peak distance.
Stage 6: Classify.What to expect: The run report and tool output show how many points were flagged and what percentage that is - 0% usually means the threshold is too high, and close to 100% usually means it's too low. When clustering is on, the report also lists how many damage sites were found and how many flagged points were rejected as isolated noise. 'Load RMS & Suggest Threshold' looks up Stage 3's saved RMS sidecar (point it at the same comparison .ply used in Stage 5, not the M3C2 result itself) and multiplies by 2-3x as a starting point - only works if Stage 3 ran with alignment and successfully found an RMS value. If no damage sites survive clustering, lower the cluster density or minimum site size, or raise the cluster gap tolerance (DBSCAN only). Keep all points: turn it on when Stage 7 must make a full surface. Stage 7 then uses all points. Stage 8 shows the flagged points as a separate layer (FlaggedPoints) and fills its field automatically in project mode.
Stage 6: Classify.Next steps: Use the output as the input to Stage 7 (Surface). With 'Keep all points' on (the default), Stage 7 makes a full surface, and Stage 8 shows the flagged points as the FlaggedPoints layer. Open the output in CloudCompare and colour it by 'classified' or 'cluster_id' to check which points were flagged and which damage site they belong to. If needed, adjust the settings and run again.

Stage 7: Surface.Purpose: Makes a triangle mesh from a point cloud, usually the classified change cloud from Stage 6. A mesh is easier to read than points in Omniverse, and gives surface-area figures for the flagged damage. Stage 7 runs blender_surface.py in Blender, with the Geometry Nodes recipe in configs\ExtraDownsampling.blend. Since update 8, this is the only method on the page: in checks on real data it was clearly better than Poisson and Ball Pivoting (Open3D).
Stage 7: Surface.Inputs:
- Blender script (blender_surface.py, in the scripts folder)
- Classified change cloud .ply (pick it with 'Choose from project...' in project mode)
- Output mesh .ply (filled automatically in project mode)
- Blender program (blender.exe). The line below the field shows 'Blender found' or 'Blender not found'.
- .blend file (recipe) and object name (optional)
- Voxel size (default 2.5 cm), Volume radius (default 1.5 cm), Delete further (default 2 cm). The defaults are the values saved in ExtraDownsampling.blend. A blank field keeps the value in the .blend file.
- Carry fields: a list of the fields in the input .ply, filled when you select the input. Each checked field is copied from the nearest input point onto each mesh vertex. By default, scalar_M3C2_distance (Stage 8 colours the mesh by it) and cluster_id (the damage site of each point) are checked when the input has them. You can check more than one field.
Stage 7: Surface.Outputs: A triangle mesh .ply with the carried fields. Each carried field is written as a decimal number with the same value (a cluster_id of 3 is written as 3.0). In project mode, this run's result is recorded on the picked diff's own surface stage entry, with the values and the carried fields that the run used.
Stage 7: Surface.What to expect:
The recipe first removes each point that has no neighbour nearer than 'Delete further'. Then it makes a volume around the remaining points (voxel size, volume radius) and makes the surface of that volume. The app puts the input points into the recipe object, runs the modifier one time, and saves the result. The app does not change the .blend file. The Terminal tab shows the values that Blender used, the vertex and face counts, and the surface area. A cloud of 3.9 million points needed 1.5 minutes and 5 GB of memory in a test.

Voxel size: a smaller value gives more detail, a slower run and a larger file. Volume radius: a larger value closes gaps between points, but moves the surface away from the points - in a test on real data, 2 cm put 11% of the points more than 5 cm from the mesh (1.5 cm: almost none). Delete further: a larger value keeps more isolated points.

If the result has no faces, the stage fails: decrease the voxel size, increase the volume radius, or increase 'Delete further'. The surface is closed around the points, so a single wall becomes a thin closed shell. To change the recipe itself, edit the .blend file in Blender 5.2 or newer and save it. If your .blend file does not have the three inputs, clear the three fields. Normals and colours of the input are not in the Carry fields list: Blender cannot carry them. Each extra carried field adds a little time (in a test, three fields took 2 seconds more than one field).
Stage 7: Surface.Next steps: Open the mesh in CloudCompare or Omniverse to check it visually, then use it as the Change-highlight input to Stage 8 (Export).

Stage 8: Export to USD.Purpose: Converts a cleaned baseline map and a change cloud or mesh into a USD scene for downstream use (e.g. Omniverse), with an optional .usdz package for web/AR/mobile viewers. Accepts either point clouds or meshes for either input independently.
Stage 8: Export to USD.Inputs:
- Path to a USD export script (defaults to usd_export.py next to the applet)
- Baseline .ply or mesh. In project mode, this auto-fills from the PROJECT's own baseline cleanup output - not anything specific to the picked diff, since the exported scene's environment layer should stay the same no matter which diff produced the change highlight.
- Change-highlight .ply or mesh. In project mode, this auto-fills from the picked diff's own Stage 7 (Surface) output.
- Optional: damage detail .ply from extract_damage_detail.py. Not a tracked project stage - always picked by hand, in both manual and project mode.
- Optional: flagged points - a Stage 6 (Classify) output. In project mode, the app fills it when the Classify run of the diff used 'Keep all points'.
- Optional: damage sites (.clusters.json) - the cluster summary that Stage 6 writes next to its output. In project mode, the app fills it from the Classify output of the diff. If you pick a Classify .ply as the change input, the app fills it from the file next to that .ply.
- Optional: surface labels - a Stage 4 (Segment) output of the reference scan of this diff. Used only with damage sites. In project mode, the app fills it with the reference cloud that Stage 5 used.
- Output .usd path
- Optional: also package as .usdz
- Optional: downsample point cloud layers via voxel size (off by default)
Stage 8: Export to USD.Outputs: A .usd scene file with /World/Compartment/Baseline (muted grey, small points or a plain-colored mesh), /World/Compartment/ChangeHighlight (blue-white-red diverging colormap driven by the M3C2 distance field, larger points or a colored mesh if the field was carried through in Stage 7), and optionally /World/Compartment/DamageDetail (real comparison-cloud geometry near flagged locations, colored the same way - shows what damage/debris actually looks like now, since ChangeHighlight is a magnitude value plotted at baseline positions, not the true current shape). If a flagged points file is given, also /World/Compartment/FlaggedPoints: only the flagged points (cluster_id 0 or more, else classified = 1), coloured like ChangeHighlight. Hide ChangeHighlight to see only the damage. If a damage sites file is given, also /World/Compartment/DamageSites: one see-through box for each damage site (Site_00, Site_01, ...), at the centre of the site and with the size of the site. The colour goes from pale orange to red; the site with the largest change is red. With surface labels, each site also shows the surface it is on, for example 'Site 03 - wall_2'. The scene is in metres (metersPerUnit = 1), with Z up and /World as the default prim. If the .usdz option is checked, also a matching .usdz package next to it.
Stage 8: Export to USD.What to expect:
Requires 'pip install usd-core plyfile' in addition to the other packages. Point-cloud output has been confirmed valid (opened and read back successfully) including in Omniverse. Mesh input is fully supported and auto-detected - Stage 7 (Surface) is now a wired pipeline stage, so a mesh no longer has to come from running surface_reconstruction.py by hand. Update 6 corrected extract_damage_detail.py: before, it stopped with 'space character(s) in name' on each run. Its field is now named scalar_M3C2_distance. When the flagged input has cluster_id, each detail point gets the cluster_id of its nearest damage site. A .usd file from before update 6 has no unit, so a viewer can show it 100 times too small - export it again. If walls block the interior view in Omniverse, try Omniverse's camera near-clip distance to see through geometry the camera is positioned inside/behind, or toggle Baseline's visibility off in the Stage panel to isolate the other layers. Downsampling (if enabled) only affects point cloud layers, not meshes - it keeps one representative point per voxel cell, removing redundant near-duplicate points from overlapping scan passes rather than real detail, as long as the voxel size stays smaller than the smallest feature you care about seeing. Useful for reducing file size and processing load in viewers like Isaac Sim.

Extract Damage Detail: this step runs extract_damage_detail.py. It uses the same running lock and Stop button as a stage run. The Radius field shows the normal scale of this diff (from Stage 5) when it is known. In project mode, the result goes into the export folder of this diff. The 'Damage detail .ply' field then shows the result.

Damage sites: select a Site_NN prim in the Omniverse Stage panel. The Property panel shows its values under 'Raw USD Properties': delta:pointCount, delta:meanMagnitude and delta:maxMagnitude (metres, without sign), delta:centroid and delta:extent (metres). The DamageSites group shows the Classify counts: delta:nFlagged, delta:nConfirmed and delta:nNoise. A flat site (for example a dent in one wall) gets a box of at least 2 cm in each direction, so that you can see it. If the file is not a cluster summary, the export stops with an error and does not write a .usd file. Surface labels: delta:surface is the surface that most points of the site are on, and delta:surfaceShare (0 to 1) is the part of the points on that surface. A low value shows a site across more than one surface, for example in a corner. The names come from the manifest.json in the same folder as the surface labels file. Extract Damage Detail with a 'Keep all points' Classify output uses only the flagged points (update 7). Before, it used all points of the surface.
Stage 8: Export to USD.Next steps: Open the .usd file in Omniverse or any USD-compatible viewer, or the .usdz in a web/AR/mobile viewer, to check the scene looks right - baseline in muted grey, change regions colored by magnitude, and (if used) DamageDetail showing the real current shape.
